9C

Key ideas

Springs

Definitions

Elastic material: a material that can store elastic potential energy and is able to return to its original shape once the energy is released
Elastic limit: the maximum deformation that can occur without causing permanent deformation
Hooke’s law: in an ideal spring, the force applied to the spring is directly proportional to its extension or compression
Ideal spring: a hypothetical spring that is considered frictionless and mass-less and that obeys Hooke’s law
Elastic potential energy: the energy stored in the material when it is deformed within its elastic limits

9C

New knowledgeElasticity

Springs

When an object compresses, extends or twists and then returns to its original shape, the material has stored energy by changing shape.

Any material that can change shape and then return to its original shape is called an elastic material.

All elastic materials have an elastic limit, this is the maximum stress that a material can be placed under without causing permanent deformation.

Many solid materials are elastic, such as rubber, neoprene and steel.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 295
9C

New knowledgeElasticity

Springs

Materials that change shape permanently when deformed only slightly are referred to as plastic materials.

Mud clay and plasticine are all examples of plastic materials.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 296
9C

New knowledgeHooke’s law

Springs

Springs are used extensively in a range of machines and devices.

Toys, pens, electronics, mattresses, medical devices, automatic watches, mining and drilling equipment and vehicles are just a few examples of where springs are used.

We have been able to utilise springs so effectively because we have known about their properties for over 300 years.

In 1676 British physicist Robert Hooke first proposed Hooke’s law, that in an ideal spring, the force applied to the spring is directly proportional to its extension or compression.

Figure 9C–4 Force versus extension graph for an ideal spring with a spring constant of k = 250 N m$^{-1}$.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 297
9C

New knowledgeHooke’s law

Springs

Imagine a specific spring resting horizontally – when no force is applied to the spring there will be no extension in the spring.

When 50 N of force is applied to this specific spring, it extends by 0.2 m; when 100 N of force is applied to the spring it extends by 0.4 m.

A force–extension graph of the spring is shown in the figure above.

The constant linear relationship between the force applied and the extension highlights Hooke’s law, that force is directly proportional to extension.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 298
9C

New knowledgeHooke’s law

Springs

The gradient of this graph is known as the spring constant, k, and as you are dividing newtons by metres the unit for the spring constant is N m−1^{-1}−1.

The gradient, and therefore the spring constant for the spring, in the graph above can be calculated as follows: gradient=k=riserun=200−00.8−0=250 N m−1\text{gradient} = k = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{200 - 0}{0.8 - 0} = 250\ \text{N m}^{-1}gradient=k=runrise​=0.8−0200−0​=250 N m−1 The spring constant gives an indication of the stiffness of the spring; the higher the spring constant, the more force is required to extend or compress the spring and therefore the stiffer it is.

For example, a spring that has a spring constant of 500 N m−1^{-1}−1 would take twice as much force to extend it an equal amount as the spring with a spring constant of 250 N m−1^{-1}−1.

This is shown in the graphs below.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 299
9C

New knowledgeHooke’s law

Springs

Hooke’s law can be represented mathematically as follows: F=−kxF = -kxF=−kx There is a negative sign to indicate that the spring’s restoring force acts in the opposite direction to the compression or extension.

For simplicity, this book will omit the negative sign from this point onwards.

This means that the formula will indicate the magnitude of the force on the spring and hence the magnitude of the force by the spring.

While the above equation only refers to springs, the relationship holds true for all solid elastic materials.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 2910
9C

New knowledgeElastic potential energy

Springs

When an elastic material is compressed, extended or twisted, it stores energy.

This stored energy is known as elastic potential energy or elastic potential energy.

When the elastic potential energy is released, the object will return to its original shape.

Imagine a spring that has a spring constant, k.

Figure 9C–6 The area under a force versus compression graph for an elastic material is the elastic potential energy.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3311
9C

New knowledgeElastic potential energy

Springs

A force–compression graph of the spring is shown on the right.

You should note that the values shown on the y-axis are a measure of force and values on the x-axis are a measure of distance (compression or extension).

This means that this graph is just a special force–distance graph, and the area under a force–distance graph is work.

This means that the area under a force–compression/extension graph is the work done to compress or extend the objects as well as the amount of elastic potential energy stored in the object.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3312
9C

New knowledgeElastic potential energy

Springs

For the force–compression graph above, the elastic potential energy would be given by the area under the triangle; therefore: elastic potential energy=Es=12(F)(x)\text{elastic potential energy} = E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}(F)(x)elastic potential energy=Es​=21​(F)(x) Hooke’s law states that F = kx.

Therefore, the force, F, in the above equation can be substituted for kx as shown: Es=12(k)(x)(x)E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}(k)(x)(x)Es​=21​(k)(x)(x) Es=12kx2E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}Es​=21​kx2

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3313
9C

New knowledgeElastic potential energy increases with extension

Springs

When trying to extend a spring, it gets harder to change the shape of the spring the more you extend it.

To extend a spring by 1 cm when it is resting does not take as much energy as extending the same spring by 1 cm when it is already stretched.

This is because the more you stretch a spring, the greater the restoring force becomes and therefore more energy must be applied to overcome this force.

This is also true when trying to compress a spring.

Figure 9C–7 The force versus extension graph for an ideal spring with spring constant k = 200 N m$^{-1}$. The energy needed to extend the spring increases the more lengthened the spring becomes.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3514
9C

New knowledgeElastic potential energy increases with extension

Springs

This is shown graphically in Figure 9C–7, with a spring that has a spring constant of 200 N m−1^{-1}−1.

As the spring extends, it takes more and more energy to extend it by the same amount.

The energy required to extend the spring by 1 cm is represented by the shaded region in the graph.

It is clear that the longer the spring becomes, the more energy is required to extend the spring by 1 cm.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3515
9C

New knowledgeElastic potential energy increases with extension

Springs

Therefore, when finding the change in elastic potential energy, you can either find the area under the graph or take away the elastic potential energy of the initial length, xix_{\text{i}}xi​, from the elastic potential energy of the final length, xfx_{\text{f}}xf​: ΔEs=12kxf2−12kxi2\Delta E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx_{\text{f}}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}kx_{\text{i}}^{2}ΔEs​=21​kxf2​−21​kxi2​

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3516
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a horizontal spring system

Springs

Imagine an ideal spring that works the same in compression and extension.

The spring is lying horizontally on a frictionless surface, with one end fixed against a wall and the other end attached to a free object.

If the object is pulled back and let go, it will oscillate about an equilibrium position.

When the object is at the equilibrium position, it will have no net force on it.

Figure 9C–8 An object attached to a horizontal spring has no net force at its equilibrium position.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3817
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a horizontal spring system

Springs

The object will have no net force on it because the spring is at its natural length, it is not compressed or extended, and the force due to gravity of the object is balanced by the normal force applied by the surface on the object.

As the spring oscillates, the kinetic energy and elastic potential energy will fluctuate between maximum values and zero.

Since the total energy, ETE_{\text{T}}ET​, will remain the same throughout the oscillation the sum of the kinetic energy, EkE_{\text{k}}Ek​, and elastic potential energy, EsE_{\text{s}}Es​, at any given point will be equal to the total energy.

This can been represented by the following formula: ET=Ek+EsE_{\text{T}} = E_{\text{k}} + E_{\text{s}}ET​=Ek​+Es​ ET=12mv2+12kx2E_{\text{T}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}ET​=21​mv2+21​kx2 Position 1: At position 1 the spring is fully extended, it is a point of maximum spring potential energy and zero kinetic energy.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3818
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a horizontal spring system

Springs

As the object moves towards the equilibrium position (2) the kinetic energy increases and the spring potential energy decreases.

Position 2: At the equilibrium positions (2 and 4) the spring will have maximum kinetic energy and zero spring potential energy.

Once the object passes the equilibrium position the spring begins to compress, slowing the object down.

The kinetic energy will decrease while the spring potential energy increases.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3819
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a horizontal spring system

Springs

Position 3: At position 3 the spring potential energy will be a maximum and the kinetic energy will be zero.

The object will then gain kinetic energy and lose spring potential energy as it moves back to the equilibrium (4).

Position 4: At the equilibrium position again the spring will have maximum kinetic energy and zero spring potential energy.

Once past the equilibrium the kinetic energy of the object will decrease and the spring potential energy will increase.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3820
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a horizontal spring system

Springs

Position 1: This decrease in kinetic energy will continue until the spring comes momentarily to rest at position 1, ready to repeat the cycle.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 3821
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a vertical spring system

Springs

For a vertical spring system, imagine an ideal spring with one end fixed to a ceiling and the other end attached to an object that is free to move.

If the object is dropped and allowed to move freely under the influence of gravity, it will oscillate about an equilibrium position.

When the object attached to a vertical spring is at the equilibrium position, it will have no forces on it.

This is because the upwards spring force will balance the downwards force due to gravity.

Figure 9C–10 An object attached to a vertical spring has no net force at its equilibrium position. The spring force $F_{\text{spring}}$ balances the weight force $F_{\text{weight}}$.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 4022
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a vertical spring system

Springs

The upwards spring force balancing the downwards force due to gravity is shown mathematically below: kx=mgkx = mgkx=mg The equilibrium position is the position of maximum kinetic energy.

As the spring oscillates about the equilibrium position, the gravitational potential energy, elastic potential energy and kinetic energy will fluctuate between maximum values and zero.

Before analysing the motion of a vertical spring system you must define the point of zero gravitational potential energy.

It will be the lowest point of the spring’s oscillation (position 3 in the diagram).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 4023
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a vertical spring system

Springs

When the object is initially dropped (position 1), the spring is in its natural position, under no compression or extension.

This means that the spring potential energy and kinetic energy are both equal to zero, while the gravitational potential energy is at a maximum.

As the object is pulled down by the force of gravity its spring potential energy and kinetic energy increase, while the gravitational potential energy decreases.

At the equilibrium positions (2 and 4), the kinetic energy is a maximum.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 4024
9C

New knowledgeEnergy transformations in a vertical spring system

Springs

Between positions 2 and 3, the object passes the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy starts to decrease, the gravitational potential energy continues to decrease, and the spring potential energy continues to increase.

At position 3 the kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy are both equal to zero, while the spring potential energy is at a maximum.

Between positions 3 and 4, the object then moves upwards, increasing both the kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy, while decreasing the spring potential energy.

At position 4, the object passes the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy starts to decrease, the gravitational potential energy continues to increase, and the spring potential energy continues to decrease, until the object returns to position 1 and the cycle repeats.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 4025
9C

New knowledgeMathematical relationships in a vertical spring system

Springs

The gravitational potential energy lost by the object will be transformed into the elastic potential energy and kinetic energy of the system.

This relationship can be represented by the formula: Eg=Es+EkE_{\text{g}} = E_{\text{s}} + E_{\text{k}}Eg​=Es​+Ek​ mgΔh=12kx2+12mv2mg\Delta h = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}mgΔh=21​kx2+21​mv2 Since the change in height is equal to the change in length of the spring, Δh can be replaced with an x as shown below: mgx=12kx2+12mv2mgx = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}mgx=21​kx2+21​mv2

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 9, p. 4226

Springs
A group of engineers is testing two springs, spring A and spring B, for use on mining equipment. The results of their tests are displayed on the force–compression graphs shown on the right.
a Calculate the spring constant of spring A and spring B and state which spring is stiffer.
b The engineers need to select a spring that is compressed by 70−80 cm when a force of 500 kN is applied to it. Which of the springs tested would be appropriate for use? Use a calculation to justify your answer.
Key idea · Hooke’s lawF=−kxF = -kxF=−kx

Working

a When looking at any graph, you must pay attention to the units. If they are not SI units, then you must convert them and then calculate the spring constant. In this example you, must convert kN into N.
kA=(70×103)−00.1−0=7.00×105 N m−1k_{\text{A}} = \frac{(70\times10^{3}) - 0}{0.1 - 0} = 7.00\times10^{5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}kA​=0.1−0(70×103)−0​=7.00×105 N m−1
kB=(45×103)−00.1−0=4.5×105 N m−1k_{\text{B}} = \frac{(45\times10^{3}) - 0}{0.1 - 0} = 4.5\times10^{5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}kB​=0.1−0(45×103)−0​=4.5×105 N m−1
Spring A is stiffer as it has a greater spring constant.
b First, rearrange Hooke’s law to make compression the subject. Then determine the compression of both springs when loaded with 500 kN.
xA=Fk=500×1037×105=0.714 mx_{\text{A}} = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{500\times10^{3}}{7\times10^{5}} = 0.714\ \text{m}xA​=kF​=7×105500×103​=0.714 m
xB=Fk=500×1034.5×105=1.11 mx_{\text{B}} = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{500\times10^{3}}{4.5\times10^{5}} = 1.11\ \text{m}xB​=kF​=4.5×105500×103​=1.11 m
Therefore, only spring A is appropriate for use.
a kA=7.00×105k_A = 7.00\times10^{5}kA​=7.00×105 N m−1^{-1}−1, kB=4.5×105k_B = 4.5\times10^{5}kB​=4.5×105 N m−1^{-1}−1, A stiffer; b spring A

Springs
A spring, initially at rest, has a force of 3.44 kN applied to it. The spring has a spring constant of 2500 N m−1^{-1}−1.
a Calculate the change in length of the spring.
b Calculate the amount of elastic potential energy stored in the spring once the force has been applied.
Key idea · Hooke’s lawF=−kxF = -kxF=−kx

Working

a Convert all units to SI units.
F=3.44×103 NF = 3.44\times10^{3}\ \text{N}F=3.44×103 N
Then rearrange the appropriate formula to make the change in length the subject. Substitute the appropriate values to solve the equation:
x=Fk=3.44×1032500=1.38 mx = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{3.44\times10^{3}}{2500} = 1.38\ \text{m}x=kF​=25003.44×103​=1.38 m
The change in length is 1.38 m.
b Select the appropriate formula and substitute the appropriate values in to solve the equation:
Es=12kx2=12(2500)(1.38)2=2.37×103 JE_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(2500)(1.38)^{2} = 2.37\times10^{3}\ \text{J}Es​=21​kx2=21​(2500)(1.38)2=2.37×103 J
a 1.38 m; b 2.37×1032.37\times10^{3}2.37×103 J

We doEnergy released by a compressed spring

Springs
A spring of length 40 cm with a spring constant of 43.5 N m−1^{-1}−1 is initially compressed to 30 cm and is then released back to a length of 35 cm. Calculate the amount of energy released when the spring is released back to a length of 35 cm.
Key idea · Hooke’s lawF=−kxF = -kxF=−kx

Working

ΔEs=12kxf2−12kxi2\Delta E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx_{\text{f}}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}kx_{\text{i}}^{2}ΔEs​=21​kxf2​−21​kxi2​
=12(43.5)(0.05)2−12(43.5)(0.1)2= \frac{1}{2}(43.5)(0.05)^{2} - \frac{1}{2}(43.5)(0.1)^{2}=21​(43.5)(0.05)2−21​(43.5)(0.1)2
=−0.163 J= -0.163\ \text{J}=−0.163 J
Note that there is a negative sign in front of the energy because the energy is being given out. If the spring was compressed by someone’s hand, then slowly released by the same hand, the spring has done work on the hand.
−0.163 J

You tryWorksheet 9C–1 Springs Q4b

Springs
Describe the energy transformations that occur when the spring is released from a position of 20 cm of extension and moves to a position of full compression.

Working

Once the spring is released from its fully extended position, the elastic potential energy will transform into kinetic energy until it reaches the equilibrium position. (1 mark)
Once the mass passes the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy begins to convert into elastic potential energy until the spring is fully compressed. (1 mark)
9C Worksheet 9C–1 Springs.docx, WS9C-4b. Working from the worksheet answers.45
9C

You tryWorksheet 9C–1 Springs Q4c

Springs
When will the maximum velocity of the mass occur? Justify your answer.

Working

The velocity will be at a maximum at the equilibrium point, when the spring is at its natural length. (1 mark)
This means that there is no net force on the mass, so the acceleration of the mass is zero. (1 mark)
Therefore, before this point, the mass would have been accelerating in the direction of travel and after this point the mass will begin to decelerate. (1 mark)

You tryWorksheet 9C–1 Springs Q5a

Springs
A spring, with a spring constant of 150 N m−1^{-1}−1, is hung vertically from a ceiling. A 5 kg mass is attached to the base of the spring and the spring is allowed to oscillate freely. For this question, ignore the effects of air resistance and friction and assume that the spring’s mass is negligible.
a When is the velocity of the mass at a maximum? Justify your answer.

Working

The velocity will be at a maximum at the equilibrium point, when the spring force is balanced by the force due to gravity. (1 mark)
At this point, the forces on the mass are balanced and the acceleration is zero. (1 mark)
Therefore, before this point, the mass would have been accelerating in the direction of travel and after this point the mass will begin to decelerate. (1 mark)

You trySection 9C questions Q6

Springs
A spring with a natural (unextended length) of 10 cm is hung vertically and a mass of 4 kg is attached to the spring, which causes it to oscillate. At the lowest point of its oscillation, the spring has a total length of 16 cm. A diagram of this situation is shown below.
a What is the length of the spring when the velocity is a maximum? Explain why this length corresponds to the maximum velocity.
b Calculate the spring constant of the spring.
c As the spring extends from 10 cm to 16 cm in length, describe the changes that occur in the gravitational potential energy of the mass and the elastic potential energy.
d What is the maximum velocity of the mass throughout the oscillation?

Working

a The total length of the spring would be 13 cm. At this point the spring force and weight force are equal
this is called the equilibrium position. The spring will accelerate towards the equilibrium position. Therefore, the moment the mass moved to the equilibrium position it must be at its maximum velocity as in the next moment the mass will move past the equilibrium position. This means the direction of acceleration will change, causing the spring to decelerate.
b When the spring is half of its maximum extension, the weight force and the spring force on the mass are equal, therefore:
mg=kxmg = kxmg=kx
k=mgxk = \frac{mg}{x}k=xmg​
=(4)(9.8)(0.03)= \frac{(4)(9.8)}{(0.03)}=(0.03)(4)(9.8)​
=1.31×103 N m−1= 1.31\times10^{3}\ \text{N m}^{-1}=1.31×103 N m−1
c When the spring has a length of 10 cm, it has maximum gravitational potential energy. The mass then falls, converting its gravitational potential energy to spring potential energy. When the spring is 16 cm in length, all of the gravitational potential energy of the mass has been converted into spring potential energy.
d Take Eg=0E_{\text{g}} = 0Eg​=0 at the equilibrium position, where the velocity will be a maximum.
EtotalE_{\text{total}}Etotal​ (release point) = EtotalE_{\text{total}}Etotal​ (equilibrium)
Eg=Es+EkE_{\text{g}} = E_{\text{s}} + E_{\text{k}}Eg​=Es​+Ek​
mgx=12kx2+12mv2mgx = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}mgx=21​kx2+21​mv2
v=2m(mgx−12kx2)v = \sqrt{\frac{2}{m}\left(mgx - \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}\right)}v=m2​(mgx−21​kx2)​
=24((4)(9.8)(0.03)−12(1.31×103)(0.03)2)= \sqrt{\frac{2}{4}\left((4)(9.8)(0.03) - \frac{1}{2}(1.31\times10^{3})(0.03)^{2}\right)}=42​((4)(9.8)(0.03)−21​(1.31×103)(0.03)2)​
=0.542 m s−1= 0.542\ \text{m s}^{-1}=0.542 m s−1

Rob and Sophia have set up an energy transfer experiment. In this experiment, a steel ball, that has a mass of 45 g, is hung from the ceiling via a piece of string and then placed next to a loaded spring. The spring is compressed by 5 cm and is held in place by a force of 0.725 N. When the spring is released, it transfers all of its energy to the steel ball, which swings up in an arc. Be able to describe the energy transformations that occur in vertical and horizontal oscillating springs
A spring fixed at one end and with a mass attached at the other end is placed horizontally on a polished surface that can be considered frictionless. The mass is then pulled, extending the spring, then released and allowed to oscillate freely. Describe the changes to elastic potential energy and kinetic energy that occur as the spring goes from a fully extended to a fully compressed position. The spring works the same in extension and compression.
When the spring is extended, the spring potential energy is at a maximum but the kinetic energy is zero. Once released, the spring potential energy will decrease as the kinetic energy increases. When the spring is at its rest length it will have no spring potential energy and the kinetic energy will be at a maximum. After this point, the spring will begin to compress and the kinetic energy will decrease, while the spring potential energy increases. Once fully compressed, the spring potential energy will be a maximum and the kinetic energy will be zero.
